doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Expressing life through the blues, not just notes
summary: Woods and Roker discuss blues as emotional expression versus classical playing, and the need for heart as well as study.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: The thing I wanted to say about that and then you kind of elaborate on this is in the African-American community it came that when you play the blues, you express yourself. You don’t just execute notes, black dots on a page. You express yourself.

With emotion. And the freedom involved in that became a kind of unspoken but musical camaraderie. In other words, when I hear you play that blues I can tell that that cost you something experientially.

Oh, yeah. you express your life, you express the way you live. You know like some people that go to school formally, I’m not saying all, but some people they tend to play too classically. So it’s something that has to be in you I believe. I think you have to be blessed. You have to be blessed. You have to have a certain talent for being able to play the blues and to really play the blues, you know, with feeling. Even though you’re playing maybe rhythm changes, but it should still swing like the blues. Like the Gospel. It should always have that feeling in there. And that’s one thing about Joe Williams that I like. You know he’s so versatile. He can sing a ballad, and it’s soulful, and he can sing an uptempo tune and it’s soulful. But he can really sing the blues. And it’s not jazz unless you have the blues instilled in there somewhere.
So you can’t learn it all out of a book.
Well it’s nice, in fact you should have something in your head too but you should also have something in your heart. And that’s what the blues come out of, you know, out of your heart.
